questions.q: What is the main problem with structuring a research report chronologically ("first I tried X, then Y, then Z")?
options: Chronological structure is always too short to be useful
It forces the reader to reconstruct the actual finding from a narrative instead of stating up front what you believe now and how strongly
It is against standard formatting rules for all technical writing
It takes longer to write than other structures
questions.explain: A chronological narrative buries the main finding inside a story of what was tried. Leading with the claim states the conclusion plainly, with the rest of the report supporting and qualifying it.

questions.q: Why should detailed methodology (exact model size, data, training budget, seed count) appear in the main body of a report rather than only in an appendix?
options: Because appendices are not allowed in technical reports
Because a reader deciding whether to trust the claim needs this detail close enough to check it without flipping away, especially anything that differs between treatment and baseline
Because methodology details are rarely important to a reader
Because appendices cannot contain numerical data
questions.explain: A skeptical reader needs to check the methodology against the claim directly. Anything that differs between the baseline and treatment besides the variable under test is the first thing a careful reader will ask about, so it needs to be visible, not buried.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend reporting per-seed values in addition to a mean and standard deviation?
options: Per-seed values are required by journal formatting standards

Per-seed values let a reader judge for themselves whether an effect looks consistent across runs or is being carried by one lucky seed, since a single run's number is close to uninformative given seed-to-seed variance
Per-seed values eliminate the need to report a mean at all
Per-seed values are only relevant for classification tasks
questions.explain: Because run-to-run variance from seed alone can be as large as many reported effects, showing individual per-seed values (not just a summary statistic) lets readers assess the consistency of the result themselves.

questions.q: What is the value of including a short 'what we tried and ruled out' section in a research report?
options: It makes the report longer, which always improves credibility
It saves a future reader starting a related project from wasting time retrying something already shown not to work -- information that is often as valuable as the headline result
It is required by all research institutions regardless of content
It replaces the need to report uncertainty on the main result
questions.explain: Reporting what didn't work gives readers information that can save significant time on related projects, and the lesson notes it's one of the highest-value additions to a report, despite often being cut under time pressure.

questions.q: Why would claiming a technique 'improves transformer training' in general, based on a 4% improvement on one benchmark at one model scale, be considered overclaiming?
options: Because a 4% improvement is too small to ever be meaningful
Because the actual evidence only supports a narrow claim about that specific setup (that model scale, that dataset, that task), not a general claim beyond the tested scope
Because transformer training results can never be reported as percentages
Because overclaiming only applies to negative results, not positive ones
questions.explain: A result from one scale, one dataset, and one task supports a claim scoped to that setup. Generalizing beyond the tested scope without evidence is overclaiming, which the lesson identifies as a key failure mode to avoid.
